title: III. The Sufferings Of A Soul, The First Ordeal
paragraphs: And so Mitya sat there, staring wildly at the people around him, not understanding what was being said to him. Suddenly he got to his feet, flung his hands up, and shouted at the top of his voice:
"I'm not guilty! I'm not guilty of that blood! I'm not guilty of my father's blood.... I meant to kill him. But I'm not guilty. Not me."
But he'd barely said this when Grushenka rushed out from behind the curtain and threw herself at the police captain's feet.

"It was my fault! Mine! My wickedness!" she cried, in a heartbreaking voice, drenched in tears, stretching her clasped hands out toward them. "He did it because of me. I tortured him and drove him to it. I tortured that poor old man too, the one who's dead now, with my wickedness, and I drove him to this! It's my fault, mine first, mine most of all, my fault!"

"Yes, it's your fault! You're the chief criminal here! You fury! You harlot! You're the one most to blame!" the police captain shouted, shaking his hand at her. But he was quickly and firmly shut down. The prosecutor practically grabbed hold of him.
"This is thoroughly irregular, Mihail Makarovitch!" he cried. "You're actively obstructing the inquiry.... You're ruining the case...." he nearly gasped.
"Follow proper procedure! Follow proper procedure!" cried Nikolay Parfenovitch, badly rattled too. "Otherwise it's simply impossible!..."
"Try us together!" Grushenka cried, frantic, still on her knees. "Punish us together. I'll go with him now, even if it's to death!"

"Grusha, my life, my blood, my holy one!" Mitya dropped to his knees beside her and held her tight in his arms. "Don't believe her," he cried, "she's not guilty of anything, of any blood, of anything at all!"

He remembered afterward that several men had to drag him bodily away from her, and that she was led out, and that when he came to himself he was sitting at the table. Beside him and behind him stood the men with the metal plates. Across the table from him sat Nikolay Parfenovitch, the investigating lawyer, urging him to drink a little water from a glass on the table.

"That will refresh you, that will calm you down. Stay calm, don't be frightened," he added, with extreme politeness. Mitya (he remembered this afterward) suddenly grew intensely fascinated by the man's big rings — one set with an amethyst, another with a bright, transparent yellow stone of great brilliance. And long afterward he remembered, with wonder, how those rings had held his attention through all those terrible hours of questioning, so that he simply couldn't tear his eyes away and dismiss them as things that had nothing whatever to do with his situation. On Mitya's left, in the seat where Maximov had been sitting earlier that evening, the prosecutor now sat, and on Mitya's right, where Grushenka had been, sat a rosy-cheeked young man in a somewhat shabby hunting jacket, with ink and paper laid out before him. This was the secretary the investigating lawyer had brought along. The police captain now stood by the window at the far end of the room, beside Kalganov, who was seated there.
"Drink some water," the investigating lawyer said softly, for the tenth time.
"I have drunk it, gentlemen, I have ... but ... come, gentlemen, crush me, punish me, decide my fate!" cried Mitya, staring at the investigating lawyer with terribly fixed, wide-open eyes.
"So you flatly deny that you are guilty of your father Fyodor Pavlovitch's death?" the investigating lawyer asked, softly but insistently.

"I am not guilty. I'm guilty of another old man's blood, but not my father's. And for that I weep! I struck the old man down, I struck him.... But it's hard to have to answer for that killing with another one too — a terrible murder I had no part in.... It's a terrible accusation, gentlemen, it knocks a man flat. But who killed my father, who killed him? Who could have killed him, if not me? It's astonishing, extraordinary, impossible."
"Yes, who could have killed him?" the investigating lawyer began, but Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor, glancing at him, turned to Mitya instead.

"You needn't trouble yourself over the old servant, Grigory Vassilyevitch. He's alive, he's recovered, and despite the terrible blows he took — by his own account and yours — there seems little doubt he'll live, or so the doctor says, at least."

"Alive? He's alive?" cried Mitya, throwing up his hands. His face lit up. "Lord, I thank Thee for the miracle Thou hast worked for me, a sinner and evildoer. That's an answer to my prayer. I've been praying all night." And he crossed himself three times. He could barely catch his breath.
"So, from this Grigory, we've received evidence about you significant enough that—" the prosecutor was going to continue, but Mitya suddenly leapt up from his chair.
"One moment, gentlemen, for God's sake, one moment; I'll run to her—"

"Excuse me, but at this moment that's quite impossible," Nikolay Parfenovitch nearly shrieked, leaping to his feet as well. Mitya was seized by the men with the metal plates, but sat back down of his own accord....

"Gentlemen, what a pity! I only wanted to see her for one minute; I wanted to tell her it's washed away, it's gone — that blood that had been weighing on my heart all night — and that I'm not a murderer anymore! Gentlemen, she's my betrothed!" he said, ecstatic and reverent, glancing round at them all. "Oh, thank you, gentlemen! Oh, in one minute you've given me a new life, a new heart!... That old man used to carry me in his arms, gentlemen. He bathed me in the tub when I was a baby of three, abandoned by everyone — he was like a father to me!..."
"And so you—" the investigating lawyer began.

"Allow me, gentlemen, allow me one moment more," Mitya cut in, resting his elbows on the table and covering his face with his hands. "Give me a moment to think, let me breathe, gentlemen. All of this is horribly upsetting, horribly. A man's not a drum, gentlemen!"
"Drink a little more water," Nikolay Parfenovitch murmured.

Mitya took his hands from his face and laughed. His eyes were confident now. He seemed completely transformed in an instant. His whole manner had changed; he was once more the equal of these men, all of whom he knew, as though they'd all just met the day before, at some social gathering, with nothing having happened. We might note, in passing, that when he'd first arrived in town, Mitya had been made very welcome at the police captain's, but lately — especially over the past month — he'd hardly called at all, and when the captain ran into him, in the street, say, Mitya had noticed that he frowned and only bowed out of politeness. His acquaintance with the prosecutor was less close, though he sometimes paid polite visits to the man's wife, a nervous, fanciful lady, without quite knowing why, and she always received him graciously and had, for some reason, taken an interest in him right up to the end. He hadn't had time to get to know the investigating lawyer, though he'd met him and spoken with him twice, each time about the fair sex.

"You're a highly skilled lawyer, I can see, Nikolay Parfenovitch," Mitya cried, laughing merrily, "but I can help you now. Oh, gentlemen, I feel like a new man, and don't take offense at my speaking to you so plainly and directly. I'm rather drunk too, I'll admit that frankly. I believe I've had the honor and pleasure of meeting you, Nikolay Parfenovitch, at my kinsman Miüsov's. Gentlemen, gentlemen, I don't pretend to be your equal. I understand perfectly well in what capacity I'm sitting before you. Oh, of course, there's a terrible suspicion ... hanging over me ... if Grigory has given evidence.... A terrible suspicion! It's awful, awful, I understand that! But to business, gentlemen, I'm ready, and we'll get it over with in a moment; because, listen, listen, gentlemen! Since I know I'm innocent, we can settle this in a minute. Can't we? Can't we?"
Mitya spoke a great deal, quickly, nervously, effusively, as though he genuinely took his listeners for his closest friends.
"So, for now, we'll record that you flatly deny the charge brought against you," Nikolay Parfenovitch said, impressively, and, leaning down to the secretary, dictated in an undertone what to write.

"Write it down? You want that written down? Well, write it; I consent, I give my full consent, gentlemen, only ... do you see?... Wait, wait, write this. Of disorderly conduct I am guilty, of violence against a poor old man I am guilty. And there's something else at the bottom of my heart I'm guilty of too — but that you needn't write down" (he turned suddenly to the secretary); "that's my private life, gentlemen, that's none of your concern, the bottom of my heart, I mean.... But of my old father's murder I am not guilty. That's a wild notion. A perfectly wild notion!... I'll prove it to you, and you'll be convinced in no time.... You'll laugh, gentlemen. You'll laugh at your own suspicion!..."

"Calm yourself, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," said the investigating lawyer, clearly trying to soothe Mitya's agitation with his own composure. "Before we go further with our inquiry, I'd like, if you'll consent to answer, to hear you confirm that you disliked your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch, that you were caught up in constant disputes with him. Just a quarter of an hour ago you exclaimed that you wanted to kill him: 'I didn't kill him,' you said, 'but I wanted to.'"
"Did I say that? Ach, that may well be, gentlemen! Yes, unhappily, I did want to kill him ... many times I wanted to ... unhappily, unhappily!"
"You wanted to. Would you be willing to explain precisely what led you to such a feeling of hatred for your parent?"

"What is there to explain, gentlemen?" Mitya shrugged sullenly, looking down. "I've never hidden my feelings. The whole town knows about it — everyone in the tavern knows. Only recently I declared them in Father Zossima's very cell.... And that same evening I beat my father. I nearly killed him, and I swore, before witnesses, that I'd come back and kill him.... Oh, a thousand witnesses! I've been shouting it aloud for the last month, anyone can tell you that!... The fact stares you in the face, speaks for itself, cries out — but feelings, gentlemen, feelings are another matter entirely. You see, gentlemen" — Mitya frowned — "it seems to me you've no right to question me about feelings. I understand you're bound by your office, I understand that perfectly, but that's my own affair, my private, intimate affair — yet ... since I've never hidden my feelings before ... in the tavern, for instance, I've talked to everyone about it, so ... so I won't make a secret of it now either. You see, I understand, gentlemen, that the facts stand terribly against me in this matter. I told everyone I'd kill him, and now, suddenly, he's been killed. So it must have been me! Ha ha! I can make allowances for you, gentlemen, I can quite make allowances. I'm floored myself, because who else could have murdered him, if not me? That's what it comes down to, isn't it? If not me, who, who? Gentlemen, I want to know, I insist on knowing!" he exclaimed suddenly. "Where was he killed? How was he killed? How, and with what? Tell me," he asked quickly, looking at the two lawyers.
"We found him in his study, lying on his back on the floor, his head crushed in," said the prosecutor.
"That's horrible!" Mitya shuddered, and, resting his elbows on the table, buried his face in his right hand.
"Let's go on," Nikolay Parfenovitch put in. "So what drove you to this feeling of hatred? You've stated in public, I believe, that it was rooted in jealousy?"
"Well, yes, jealousy. And not only jealousy."
"Disputes over money?"
"Yes, over money too."
"There was a dispute, I believe, over three thousand roubles, which you claimed as part of your inheritance?"

"Three thousand! More, more," Mitya cried, heatedly, "more than six thousand, more than ten, perhaps. I told everyone so, shouted it at them. But I made up my mind to settle for three thousand. I was desperate for that three thousand ... so the bundle of notes for three thousand that I knew he kept under his pillow, ready for Grushenka, I considered simply stolen from me. Yes, gentlemen, I looked on it as mine, my own property...."
The prosecutor gave the investigating lawyer a meaningful look, and managed a sly wink at him.
"We'll come back to that subject later," the lawyer said promptly. "You'll allow us to note this point and write it down — that you regarded that money as your own property?"

"Write it down, by all means. I know that's another fact against me, but I'm not afraid of facts, and I'll bring them out against myself. Do you hear me? Do you know, gentlemen, you take me for a different kind of man than I am," he added, suddenly gloomy, dejected. "You're dealing with a man of honor, a man of the highest honor — above all, don't lose sight of that — a man who's done plenty of vile things, but who's always been, and still is, honorable at bottom, in his inner being. I don't know how to put it. That's exactly what's made my whole life wretched, that I longed to be honorable, that I was, so to speak, a martyr to a sense of honor, hunting for it with a lantern, Diogenes' lantern, and yet all my life I've been doing filthy things, like all of us, gentlemen ... that is, like me alone. That was the mistake — like me alone, me alone!... Gentlemen, my head aches..." His brows knit in pain. "You see, gentlemen, I couldn't bear the sight of him — there was something in him base, insolent, trampling on everything sacred, something mocking and irreverent, loathsome, loathsome. But now that he's dead, I feel differently."
"How do you mean?"
"I don't feel differently, exactly, but I wish I hadn't hated him so much."
"You feel penitent?"
"No, not penitent, don't write that down. I'm not much good myself, I'm nothing beautiful to look at, so I had no right to find him repulsive. That's what I mean. Write that down, if you like."
Saying this, Mitya grew very mournful. He'd been growing gloomier and gloomier as the inquiry went on.

At that moment another unexpected scene unfolded. Though Grushenka had been removed, she hadn't been taken far — only to the room two doors down from the blue room where the examination was underway. It was a small room with one window, just beyond the large room where they'd danced and feasted so lavishly. She sat there with no one but Maximov beside her, terribly downcast, terribly frightened, clinging to her side as though for safety. At their door stood one of the peasants with a metal plate on his chest. Grushenka was crying, and suddenly her grief overwhelmed her — she jumped up, flung her arms out, and, with a loud wail of sorrow, rushed out of the room toward him, toward her Mitya, so suddenly that no one had time to stop her. Mitya, hearing her cry, trembled, sprang up, and with a shout rushed headlong to meet her, not knowing what he was doing. But they weren't allowed to reach each other, though they saw one another. He was seized by the arms. He struggled, tried to tear himself free. It took three or four men to hold him. She was seized too, and he saw her stretching her arms out to him, crying aloud as they carried her away. When it was over, he came back to himself, sitting in the same spot as before, across from the investigating lawyer, and crying out to them:
"What do you want with her? Why are you tormenting her? She's done nothing, nothing!..."
The lawyers tried to calm him down. About ten minutes passed like this. At last Mihail Makarovitch, who'd been out of the room, hurried back in and said, loudly and excitedly, to the prosecutor:
"She's been taken away, she's downstairs. Will you allow me, gentlemen, to say one word to this unhappy man? In your presence, gentlemen, in your presence."
"By all means, Mihail Makarovitch," the investigating lawyer answered. "In this case, we have no objection."

"Listen, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, my dear fellow," the police captain began, his excited face showing warm, almost fatherly, feeling toward the unlucky prisoner. "I took your Agrafena Alexandrovna downstairs myself, and left her in the care of the landlord's daughters, and that old fellow Maximov's staying with her the whole time. And I comforted her, do you hear? I comforted her and calmed her down. I made it clear to her that you need to clear your name, so she mustn't get in your way, mustn't weigh you down, or you might lose your head and say the wrong thing in your testimony. I talked it all through with her, and she understood. She's a sensible girl, my boy, a good-hearted girl — she'd have kissed my old hands, begging me to help you. She sent me herself to tell you not to worry about her. And now I must go, my dear fellow, I must go and tell her that you're calm and at peace about her. So you must be calm, do you understand? I was unfair to her; she's a Christian soul, gentlemen, yes, I tell you, she's a gentle soul, not to blame for anything. So what shall I tell her, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? Will you sit quietly, or not?"

The good-natured police captain said a great deal that was highly irregular, but Grushenka's suffering — a fellow creature's suffering — touched his kindly heart, and tears stood in his eyes. Mitya jumped up and rushed toward him.

"Forgive me, gentlemen, oh, allow me, allow me!" he cried. "You have the heart of an angel, an angel, Mihail Makarovitch, I thank you for her sake. I will, I will be calm, cheerful even. Tell her, out of the kindness of your heart, that I'm cheerful, quite cheerful, that I'll be laughing in a moment, knowing she has a guardian angel like you. I'll be done with all this soon, and the moment I'm free, I'll go to her, she'll see, let her wait. Gentlemen," he said, turning to the two lawyers, "now I'll open my whole soul to you; I'll pour it all out. We'll finish this off directly, finish it off cheerfully. We'll laugh about it in the end, won't we? But, gentlemen, that woman is the queen of my heart. Oh, let me tell you that. That much I'll tell you right now.... I can see I'm among honorable men. She is my light, she is my holy one, and if only you knew! Did you hear her cry, 'I'll go to death with you'? And what have I, a penniless beggar, ever done for her? Why such love for me? How can a clumsy, ugly brute like me, with this ugly face of mine, deserve love like that, love that would send her into exile with me? And how she threw herself at your feet for my sake, just now!... and yet she's proud, and she's done nothing wrong! How can I help adoring her, how can I help crying out and rushing to her, the way I did just now? Gentlemen, forgive me! But now, now I'm comforted."

And he sank back into his chair and, covering his face with his hands, burst into tears. But they were happy tears. He recovered himself at once. The old police captain looked well pleased, and so did the lawyers. They sensed the examination had moved into a new phase. When the police captain left the room, Mitya was positively cheerful.

"Now, gentlemen, I'm at your disposal, entirely at your disposal. And if it weren't for all these trivial details, we'd understand one another in a minute. There I go again, on about details. I'm at your disposal, gentlemen, but I'll say this: we must trust one another, you in me and I in you, or there'll be no end to it. I say this for your own good. To business, gentlemen, to business, and don't go digging around in my soul; don't badger me over trifles, just ask me about the facts, about what matters, and I'll satisfy you at once. And damn the details!"
So spoke Mitya. The interrogation began again.
